questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a place which was as different as possible from Denmark (but within EU, due to Corona). Besides this, the opportunities for english classes and proper information in english also ended up playing a surprisingly large role in my decision. I had never been to Rome before my exchange, so the decision was also based a lot on the many nice things i had heard about the city from friends and family.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Rome is amazing to live in, and it has been amazing getting to know the city so well. Besides this, what mattered the most have been all the nice people i have met there. The academic level was very low, but that just meant that there was more time for all the fun things.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy. There are a lot of different systems, and signing up for the classes was a bit chaotic. The exchange office was however very helpfull and fast at answering e-mails.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Online information event and various emails. There are also an ESN erasmus-welcome-programme, but they do not offer any guidance on school-related things.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I might have answered differently if i had been asked right at the beginning. But it all worked out in the end. I was rather frustrated with the sign-up for the classes, because you had to work accross 4 or five different systems, but we all managed.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: We where four people from Denmark who found an apartment together. We found it in a group on Facebook. This might be a bit risky, since there are a lot of scams around. But it worked out very well for us, and we have all been very fond of living in the apartment. We were lucky that we got our deposit back without problems, but it seemed like most people did not. So i would recommend asking the previous renters of the apartment if they received it back, and otherwise maybe consider not paying the last months rent, which seems to be a thing in Rome.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There are not a possibility to live on Campus. The areas of Bologna and San Lorenzo are big student areas, and a bit cheaper than other places. San Lorenzo is also very noisy, though. We lived around 6 km from our campus, and it took around an hour to get there by public transportation. Due to half of the classes being online, this did not matter that much. But i can imagine that it might have been a big advantage living closer to the campus, if you have to go there every day. If you live far away, make sure it is close to a metro, the busses and trams are absolutely unreliable. Also, i liked living quite central (within the walls, we lived right next to the Aventine Hill, around 1 km. below Circus Maximus). Public transportation is not always too great, especially not at night, so it was very nice being able to walk to most places and to live at a place which was quite well-connected.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is a bit cheaper than Copenhagen standards. It is very Italien in the way that most people experience things that does not work and are never really fixed properly. Also all apartments are very cold during winter/fall. But that is just part of the experience i suppose.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As i wrote earlier, rather confusing.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You have to make sure yourself, that there are not clashes with both time-schedules and exams. And the exam-dates are not published before quite a few weeks after the start of the semester. In WebSelf service you can check which group you are in, on this page
https://www.luiss.edu/cattedreonline
you can check the "syllabus" of the different available classes. You also sign up in WebSelf service as far as i remember. And then there is an equivalent to absalon called "luisslearn". You can change the classes for a long time, also after they have started, so do not panic if you sign up to something wrong.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Erasmus office, with a very helpfull lady called Roberta Limone, whom answers mails very fast and precise.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed. Luckily you can change it, also several weeks into the semester.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take a deep breath and remember that all classes are taught twice a week, so when making your schedule, remember to put both in there, so you don't end up with clashes. Also, do not expect to end up with the classes you have picked in your pre-approval, you have to choose them at least three times more. And write an email to Roberta Limone or her equivalent in case of any doubts.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would not call it academic. I made simulation-games where i had to pretend i where India in the UN, UAE in the cop26 or something similar around 4 times. Do not waste your time reading the texts unless you find it funny, you are only examined in the words of the teachers.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: As mentioned it was very low. I think i might have also managed to pick some of the worst ones - some of the EU-classes might have been a bit better. But certainly do not go there for the academics. They do not use citations, and i was several times asked to not put in references. A teacher at first said that he "did not understand why we kept asking for a book" when we asked where the syllabus where. Some classes are mainly historical facts, some try with a few theories, but on a very low level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: MANY student presentations. Which are not 10-minute ones but one and a half hour. Simulation-games takes up a lot of time. One class was without power-point and without texts, so you had to write everything down (I would not recommend "international organizations and human rights" for this reason). But other than that just normal teacher-presentations.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Sociology of terrorism, international organization of human rights, diplomacy and negotiation, chinese studies and geopolitical scenarios.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: None of them really. Chinese studies where very easy and the teacher was very sweet, so maybe that one. Sociology of terrorism was interesting enough, but the teacher is really not very pleasent. Diplomacy and negotiation was relatively okay, but we spend around a month on simulation games. Geopolitical scenarios was just the teachers view on world history (fun fact, Brexit is the fault of the queen of England and France should just share their nuclear weapons with the rest of Europe). International organization and human rights is the most boring class i have ever had, and the teacher Elena Scico laughs at people at their exam. Maybe try the EU-courses. I had only oral exams, and they are in front of the whole class and absolut chaos. It is not as bad as it sounds, but if you are not into oral exams, maybe consider taking a few ones with a written exam. It is hard to avoid having a few orals, but they are really not that bad.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I just think i spend more money than i expected, i am not quite sure that i can explain on what. We also did quite a few trips around the country, and traveling back and forth for Christmas was also a bit expensive. But it kind of all added up with various scholarships.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Supermarkets are more expensive than expected. Drinks are much cheaper some places, beers are more expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The ESN intro-programme was not that exciting, just a lot of parties in weird clubs. Might have been more fun if it was not corona and you where allowed to stand up and dance and such things. There where sports-clubs, but the information about them was not that good. But i would recommend signing up for a sports-team, it seemed nice!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Some sports-clubs, but i do not know much about it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a sport-team. Participate in the intro-programme even though it is a bit silly and expensive.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Take trips and spend time on just getting to know Rome.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy. I had some frustrations about the teaching methods and the teachers attitudes, but the other students very very nice.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: They are very friendly, maybe join some clubs out of class if you want to get to know some Italians.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The professors. For instance being 20 min late for an exam, being on the phone during exams and generally much more hierarchy. I had a hard time accepting to call people "professor" (especially when they are actually not professors...). Also Italians are generally really not hiding their feelings, and i got told off but random Italians quite a few times.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Very friendly and helpfull students, and the laid-back italian attitude to many things. Met a very lot of very nice italian people, they do not seem as busy as we do.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. It is an amazing experience, please do it. 2. Do not expect too much of the academic level, but try to take the differences as an experience. 3. Enjoy it, and enjoy Rome, it is a great city to be an exchange student in!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The language-cause on LUISS is very bad. We hired a personal teacher, which was not very expensive.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the nice people, experiencing a different culture, experiencing Rome, seeing the different approach to many things.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: There where really not many challenges. I had three oral exams in two days, that  was a bit challenging. Other then that, it went quite smooth.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: By all means go on exchange and go to LUISS, it has been a really great experience and all ways. LUISS is a private business university, so the facilities are very fancy.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
